messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Vulnerability: Being naked, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Nguyen was forty-six years old, a software engineer who now worked from a spare bedroom in his suburban home, a decision he had made gradually and without ever quite stating to himself that it was necessary. Before the deployment, he had enjoyed the open-plan office, the background hum of conversation, the rhythm of colleagues moving past his desk. That felt like another life. The one that mattered now began on a reconnaissance mission in a dusty, indistinct valley, when the vehicle ahead of him hit an improvised explosive device. He was thrown from his own Humvee, the blast tearing away most of his gear and shredding the upper half of his uniform. Dazed, half-blind with dust, he found himself sprawled on the ground, his torso exposed to the sun and to whatever else might be coming. Then he heard it: the high-pitched, sputtering drone of a motorcycle engine approaching from the east, growing louder. He could smell diesel and something acrid—burning rubber, or maybe flesh—and he lay there, unable to move, convinced that the next moments would be his last. He was certain that being half-naked, without even a weapon within reach, made him nothing more than a target. The motorcycle did not stop; it passed on some parallel track, but the sound stayed inside his head like a splinter.

For months after returning home, Minh told no one about those seconds. He could not find the words to describe what had happened—when his wife, Leanne, asked how he was, he said “fine” and turned away, because the event itself refused to be shaped into sentences. It came back to him as a loop, a film that played without his permission: the blast, the sky tumbling, the exposed skin on his chest, and then that engine noise, always the same, always building toward something that never came but might next time. He began to notice that certain smells—gasoline, charred food, even the faint metallic scent of a freshly opened can—could make him stop mid-sentence, his heart thudding against his ribs. He stopped watching television altogether, because any programme that showed combat or even a news report about an overseas conflict would bring the loop roaring back. He unsubscribed from streaming services, then stopped checking the news online. When Leanne wanted to watch a drama set in a war zone, he left the room and sat in the dark of the garage until she finished.

The avoidance spread. Going out became a calculation of risk. He avoided unfamiliar places because, as he told himself, he could not assess the danger without knowing every exit, every possible hiding spot, every source of a sudden sound. Even a trip to a new grocery store felt like walking into an ambush. When strangers approached him—a cashier who stepped too close, a jogger who called out from behind—he felt a spike of alertness that was hard to control. He began to work from home, citing a need for focus, but the truth was that commuting meant passing construction sites with loud machinery, and the office itself had become unbearable: the open layout left too many approaches, too many people he could not see coming. He also stopped exercising. Running had once been his outlet, but now the pounding of his own feet, the heavy breathing, and the sensation of his heart racing all felt too close to the panic of that day. He used to run on a trail near his house, but after a cyclist passed him from behind without warning, he quit entirely.

At home he remained on guard. He sat with his back to a wall, checked the locks repeatedly, and woke at every creak of the house settling. He knew, rationally, that the suburbs were quiet, but rationality had little to do with what his body did. He would catch himself listening for a motorcycle engine that wasn’t there, then hearing it anyway in the static of his own memory. His marriage was strained: Leanne wanted to go out to dinner, visit friends in a neighbouring town, take a weekend trip—none of which he could tolerate. He saw the disappointment in her eyes and understood that he was failing her, but the thought of an unfamiliar restaurant, unpredictable smells, strangers at nearby tables, and the long drive home after dark was enough to flood him with dread.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a Tuesday evening when he could not bring himself to open the front door to retrieve a package. He stood in the hallway, hands trembling, the cardboard box only ten feet away, while a neighbour walked a dog past the driveway. Minh could not make his legs move. After ten minutes he asked Leanne to get it, and she did, silently. That night she told him she loved him but she could not watch him shrink any further. Minh agreed to come to therapy, though he was terrified that talking about what happened would only make the film play louder. What he hoped for, still too fragile to say aloud, was a single day when the smell of diesel might not feel like the start of an ending.
